planting.note: Sow seed indoors on well-drained mineral mix in late winter, then move seedlings outside after the last frost into a bed with sharp drainage and reflected heat.

directions: Sow seed indoors on well-drained mineral mix in late winter, then move seedlings outside after the last frost into a bed with sharp drainage and reflected heat. This cylindrical, banded-spine cactus from the Chihuahuan Desert produces enormous, fragrant flowers in shades of yellow, peach, or magenta that open for several days in succession each spring. It is typically solitary or forms only a few stems, making it a striking specimen plant for a xeriscape bed or trough. Give it a gravel mulch and minimal summer water to mimic its native rocky slopes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow seed on sterile gritty mix indoors in late winter, providing bottom heat, and expect slow, uneven germination typical of this notoriously slow-growing species.

directions: Sow seed on sterile gritty mix indoors in late winter, providing bottom heat, and expect slow, uneven germination typical of this notoriously slow-growing species. Cottontop cactus forms clusters of ribbed, barrel-shaped stems topped with dense white-woolly spines that give the plant its snowy, cottony crown, especially striking against its native Mojave and Sonoran Desert gravel flats. It is best suited to experienced growers with hot, extremely well-drained sites, since it resents both winter wet and heavy soil. Use it sparingly as a textural accent among boulders rather than as a fast-filling landscape plant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow seed indoors in late winter on sterile cactus mix, then transplant outdoors in spring once temperatures stay reliably mild; best near the coast or in a protected microclimate inland.

directions: Sow seed indoors in late winter on sterile cactus mix, then transplant outdoors in spring once temperatures stay reliably mild. Native to coastal bluffs and mesas of San Diego County and northern Baja California, this compact, barrel-shaped cactus bears yellow-green flowers that often have a reddish throat, blooming in late winter to early spring. It is one of the more cold-sensitive barrel cacti and does best near the coast or in a protected microclimate inland. Plant it in decomposed granite or sandy soil for the sharp drainage it needs to avoid rot.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on sterile, well-drained mix in late winter, then transplant outdoors after the last frost into a spot with excellent drainage.

directions: Start seed indoors on sterile, well-drained mix in late winter, then transplant outdoors after the last frost into a spot with excellent drainage. Remarkably cold-hardy for a cactus, this diminutive, low-growing species ranges as far north as the northern Great Plains, producing pale yellow-green flowers in spring followed by bright red-orange fruit that often persists through winter. It is well suited to rock gardens and troughs even in colder climates where most cacti fail. Plant it in a raised, gritty bed to shed winter moisture, which is more likely to harm it than cold temperatures.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Propagate by gently separating rooted offsets in spring and setting them into fast-draining, rocky soil without burying the chalky rosette; never touch or hose off the powdery bloom, which protects the leaves from sun.

directions: Propagate by gently separating rooted offsets in spring and setting them into fast-draining, rocky soil without burying the chalky rosette, or start fresh seed in cool weather on the soil surface. This striking Baja California native carries the thickest natural white-chalk coating of any succulent, and that powdery bloom should never be touched or hosed off since it protects the leaves from intense sun. It goes dormant and can shrink in the heat of summer, so water sparingly during that period and increase moisture slightly during the cooler growing season. Site it on a slope or in a container where excess water drains away instantly from the crown.
